questions.stem: With an interest-only loan, what is owed at the end of the term?
options: The whole of the original principal
Nothing, as it has all been repaid
Only the interest for the final period
Half of the original principal
questions.explanation: Interest-only repayments cover the interest each period but none of the principal, so the full amount borrowed is still owed at the end. That is why a sinking fund or another source of money is needed to repay it.

questions.stem: A sinking fund, used alongside an interest-only loan, is:
options: a fee charged by the lender for early repayment of the loan
an account where the lender holds the borrower's deposit
a savings annuity built up to repay the principal at the end
a second loan taken out to pay the interest each month
questions.explanation: The borrower makes regular deposits into a sinking fund, a future-value annuity, so that it grows to the principal by the end of the loan. The loan itself is then repaid in one payment from the fund.

questions.stem: With a reducing-balance loan, each regular repayment:
options: pays the interest due and reduces the principal
pays only the interest charged that period
pays an equal share of interest and principal
reduces the principal before any interest is due
questions.explanation: Interest is charged on the balance owing, and the rest of the repayment reduces the principal, so the balance falls steadily to zero. A repayment that covers only interest belongs to an interest-only loan.

questions.stem: Early in a 25-year home loan, most of each monthly repayment goes towards:
options: reducing the principal owed on the loan
fees and charges added by the lender
a sinking fund to repay the principal
the interest on the large balance owing
questions.explanation: At the start the balance is at its largest, so the interest charged each month is large and only a small part of the repayment reduces the principal. Later the balance is smaller, so more of each repayment goes to principal.

questions.stem: An offset account linked to a home loan reduces interest because:
options: its balance is paid to the lender each month as an extra repayment
it removes all fees and charges from the loan for its whole term
its balance is subtracted from the loan before interest is charged
it earns a higher rate of interest than the loan is charged
questions.explanation: Interest on the loan is calculated on the loan balance minus the offset balance, so money kept in the offset account saves interest at the loan rate while still being available to the borrower.

questions.stem: A loan's comparison rate takes into account:
options: only the interest rate and the term of the loan
the interest rate adjusted for inflation
the interest rate together with fees and charges
the interest rate charged after income tax
questions.explanation: A comparison rate combines the interest rate with the loan's fees and charges into a single rate, so loans with different fee structures can be compared. A loan with a low advertised rate but high fees can have a higher comparison rate than its rival.

questions.stem: Which statement about a variable-rate loan is correct?
options: The rate can rise or fall during the loan, changing the repayments
The rate is set at the start and cannot change for the whole term
The rate always rises each year by a fixed percentage
The rate is the same as the comparison rate for that loan
questions.explanation: A variable rate moves with the lender's rates, so repayments or the term can change. A fixed rate is locked for an agreed period, which gives certainty but can cost more if rates fall.

questions.stem: Which of these will reduce the total interest paid on a reducing-balance loan?
options: Making a smaller repayment each month
Moving to a loan with a higher rate
Making extra repayments whenever possible
Extending the term of the loan by 5 years
questions.explanation: Extra repayments reduce the balance sooner, so less interest is charged on it for the rest of the loan. A longer term or smaller repayments leave a larger balance owing for longer, which increases total interest.

questions.stem: A $25 000 personal loan is taken at 9% p.a. compounded monthly, repaid monthly over 5 years. What is the monthly repayment?
questions.explanation: With i = 0.0075 and n = 60, the repayment is 25 000 × 0.0075/(1 − 1.0075^−60) = $518.96. $604.17 charges flat interest on the full $25 000 for all 5 years, ignoring the falling balance.

questions.stem: A $25 000 personal loan at 9% p.a. compounded monthly is repaid at $518.96 a month for 5 years. How much interest is paid in total?
questions.explanation: Total repaid is 60 × $518.96 = $31 137.60, so the interest is $31 137.60 − $25 000 = $6137.60. $11 250 is flat interest at 9% on the whole amount for 5 years.

questions.stem: A $25 000 personal loan at 9% p.a. compounded monthly is repaid at $518.96 a month for 5 years. How much is still owed after 2 years?
questions.explanation: The balance after 24 repayments is 25 000 × 1.0075^24 − 518.96 × (1.0075^24 − 1)/0.0075 = $16 319.57. Subtracting 24 repayments from $25 000 ignores the interest charged, so it understates the debt.

questions.stem: A $450 000 home loan at 6% p.a. compounded monthly is repaid monthly over 25 years. What is the monthly repayment?
questions.explanation: With i = 0.005 and n = 300, the repayment is 450 000 × 0.005/(1 − 1.005^−300) = $2899.36. $2250.00 is the first month's interest alone, which would never reduce the balance.

questions.stem: A $450 000 home loan at 6% p.a. compounded monthly is repaid at $2899.36 a month for 25 years. What is the total interest paid?
questions.explanation: Total repaid is 300 × $2899.36 = $869 808.00; subtracting the $450 000 borrowed gives $419 808.00 interest. $869 808.00 is the total repaid, not the interest.

questions.stem: A $450 000 loan at 6% p.a. compounded monthly could be repaid over 25 years or over 20 years. About how much total interest does the 20-year term save?
questions.explanation: Over 20 years the repayment is $3223.94, total interest $323 745.54; over 25 years the total interest is $419 806.89. The saving is $96 061.35, even though each repayment is $324.58 higher.

questions.stem: A $450 000 loan at 6% p.a. compounded monthly has a repayment of $2899.36 for 25 years. If $200 extra is paid every month, about how many monthly repayments are needed?
questions.explanation: Solving with a repayment of $3099.36 gives n = 259.54, so 260 repayments, the last one smaller. That is more than 3 years sooner than the original 300 repayments.

questions.stem: Instead of $2899.36 monthly on a $450 000 loan at 6% p.a. for 25 years, half that amount is paid every fortnight, with interest compounded fortnightly. About how long does the loan now take?
options: 25 years
12.5 years
24 years
21 years
questions.explanation: Paying $1449.68 with i = 0.06/26 needs about 547 fortnights, which is about 21.0 years. Half the monthly amount every fortnight gives 26 half-payments, the same as 13 monthly payments a year, so the loan finishes about 4 years early.

questions.stem: After 5 years of repaying $2899.36 a month on a $450 000 loan at 6% p.a. compounded monthly, $404 694.39 is owed. A $20 000 lump sum is paid off and repayments continue. About how many more repayments are needed?
questions.explanation: The new balance is $384 694.39. Solving for n with a repayment of $2899.36 gives 218.32, so 219 more repayments, the last smaller, instead of the remaining 240.

questions.stem: After 3 years of a 25-year, $450 000 loan at 6% p.a. compounded monthly, $424 456.85 is owed. The rate rises to 7% p.a. What monthly repayment now clears the loan on time?
questions.explanation: The remaining 22 years are 264 months, so the repayment is 424 456.85 × (0.07/12)/(1 − (1 + 0.07/12)^−264) = $3155.51. $2999.97 wrongly spreads the balance over a fresh 25 years.

questions.stem: An investor takes a $300 000 interest-only loan at 6.6% p.a. compounded monthly. What is the monthly repayment?
questions.explanation: The monthly interest is 300 000 × 0.066/12 = $1650, and an interest-only repayment is exactly the interest. $19 800 is the yearly interest, and $3421.72 is a 10-year reducing-balance repayment.

questions.stem: To repay a $300 000 interest-only loan in 10 years, monthly deposits are made into a sinking fund paying 4.8% p.a. compounded monthly. What is the monthly deposit?
questions.explanation: The fund is a future-value annuity reaching $300 000 with i = 0.004 and n = 120: deposit = 300 000 × 0.004/(1.004^120 − 1) = $1952.72. $2500 is 300 000/120, which ignores the interest the fund earns.

questions.stem: A $300 000 interest-only loan at 6.6% p.a. compounded monthly is to be repaid from a sinking fund that needs $1952.72 a month. What is the borrower's total monthly outlay?
questions.explanation: Each month the borrower pays the loan interest of $1650 and makes the sinking fund deposit of $1952.72, a total of $3602.72. Paying only one of the two leaves either the interest or the principal unpaid.

questions.stem: Why might a business choose an interest-only loan with a sinking fund rather than a reducing-balance loan?
options: The principal is reduced faster in the early years
The lender reduces the interest rate each year
Lower repayments to the lender keep cash available
The total interest paid to the lender is always lower
questions.explanation: Paying only interest keeps the loan repayment low and gives the borrower control of the money saved in the fund. Because the principal is never reduced, the total interest paid to the lender is higher than on a reducing-balance loan.

questions.stem: A $400 000 home loan is charged 6% p.a. compounded monthly, and $30 000 sits in a linked offset account. How much interest is charged for the month?
questions.explanation: Interest is charged on 400 000 − 30 000 = $370 000, so 370 000 × 0.005 = $1850. Without the offset the interest would be $2000, so the offset saves $150 this month.

questions.stem: Rates are expected to rise. Which choice protects a borrower's repayments from the rise?
options: Fixing the rate for the next few years
Keeping the loan on a variable rate
Extending the term of the loan
Closing the linked offset account
questions.explanation: A fixed rate locks in the repayment for the fixed period, so rate rises do not affect it. The cost is that the borrower misses out if rates fall instead, and fixed loans often limit extra repayments.

questions.stem: Which strategy reduces the interest on a loan without changing the repayment amount?
options: Increasing the term of the loan by 5 years
Switching from fortnightly to monthly payments
Adding the set-up fee to the loan balance
Keeping savings in a linked offset account
questions.explanation: Money in an offset account lowers the balance on which interest is charged, so more of each repayment goes to principal. Monthly instead of fortnightly payments, a longer term or adding fees to the balance all increase the interest.

questions.stem: Paying half the monthly repayment every fortnight shortens a loan mainly because:
options: each payment is credited before interest is due
26 half-payments a year equal 13 monthly repayments
fortnightly compounding charges less interest each year
the lender lowers the rate for frequent payments
questions.explanation: A year has 26 fortnights, so half-payments add up to 13 monthly repayments instead of 12, an extra repayment each year that goes straight to principal. The slightly earlier payments help too, but the extra repayment is the main effect.

questions.stem: A $20 000 loan at 8% p.a. compounded monthly over 3 years has a $500 set-up fee and a $10 monthly fee. To find the comparison rate, how are the fees treated?
options: Both fees are ignored, as they are not interest
$500 is added to the loan amount and $10 to each repayment
$500 is added to each repayment and $10 to the loan amount
Both fees are added to the loan amount before interest
questions.explanation: The one-off set-up fee is added to the initial present value, and the ongoing charge is added to the regular payment. The rate that makes those payments repay the $20 000 actually received is the comparison rate.

questions.stem: A $20 000 loan at 8% p.a. compounded monthly over 3 years has a $500 set-up fee added to the loan and a $10 monthly fee, making each payment $652.40. Which is the comparison rate?
questions.explanation: Solving 20 000 = 652.40 × (1 − (1 + i)^−36)/i gives i × 12 = 10.75% p.a. The fees push the true cost well above the 8% advertised rate. 9.69% counts the set-up fee but leaves out the monthly fee.

questions.stem: Loan A is advertised at 6.2% p.a. with a comparison rate of 6.9% p.a. Loan B is advertised at 6.5% p.a. with a comparison rate of 6.6% p.a. Ignoring other features, which loan is likely cheaper?
options: Both cost the same over the term
B, as its comparison rate is lower
A, as its advertised rate is lower
A, as its fees make up a smaller share
questions.explanation: The comparison rate includes fees and charges, so the lower comparison rate signals the lower overall cost. A's low advertised rate hides higher fees, which is why its comparison rate is 0.7% above its advertised rate.

questions.stem: Why can a loan's comparison rate differ from the actual cost to a particular borrower?
options: It is calculated after the loan is repaid
It assumes a standard loan amount and term
It leaves out the interest rate completely
It is set by each borrower's income tax rate
questions.explanation: A comparison rate is worked out for a standard amount and term, so fees can weigh more or less heavily on a different loan. It also cannot allow for later rate changes or for fees triggered by events such as early repayment.

questions.stem: A $15 000 car loan has repayments of $480 a month for 3 years. What is the total cost of the loan above the amount borrowed?
questions.explanation: Total repaid is 36 × $480 = $17 280.00, so the interest and charges cost $2280.00 above the $15 000 borrowed. $17 280.00 is the total repaid, including the principal.

questions.stem: Saving $500 a month for a $12 000 car would take 2 years. Borrowing now costs $560 a month for 2 years. Which statement is correct?
options: Borrowing and saving cost the same over 2 years
Borrowing costs $1440 more, but the car is used 2 years sooner
Borrowing costs $60 more in total over the 2 years
Saving costs more, as the car's price rises with inflation by $1440
questions.explanation: Borrowing costs 24 × $560 = $13 440, which is $1440 more than the $12 000 price; the benefit is having the car now. $60 is the extra each month, not in total. Whether the car's price rises depends on inflation, which the scenario does not give.

questions.stem: When working out the outstanding balance of a loan after some repayments, the balance is:
options: the original principal minus the total interest paid
the amount still owed on the principal at that time
the total of all repayments still to be made
the interest still to be paid over the remaining term
questions.explanation: The outstanding balance is the debt remaining, the amount that would clear the loan if paid now. The total of the remaining repayments is larger, because it also includes the future interest.

questions.stem: Increasing a loan's term from 20 to 30 years, with the same amount and rate, will:
options: lower each repayment but raise the total interest
lower each repayment and lower the total interest
raise each repayment and raise the total interest
leave the repayment the same but cut the interest
questions.explanation: Spreading the loan over more repayments makes each one smaller, but the balance falls more slowly, so interest is charged on a larger amount for longer and the total interest rises.

questions.stem: On a $450 000 loan at 6% p.a. compounded monthly with repayments of $2899.36, by how much does the first repayment reduce the principal?
questions.explanation: The first month's interest is 450 000 × 0.005 = $2250, so only $2899.36 − $2250 = $649.36 goes to the principal. The $2250 is the interest part of the repayment.

questions.stem: A couple can afford $2500 a month. At 6% p.a. compounded monthly over 25 years, what is the most they can borrow?
questions.explanation: The loan is the present value of the repayments: 2500 × (1 − 1.005^−300)/0.005 = $388 017.16. $750 000 is the total of the repayments, which includes the interest.

questions.stem: Halfway through a 25-year reducing-balance home loan, the balance owing is:
options: exactly half of the amount borrowed
less than half of the amount borrowed
the same as the amount borrowed
more than half of the amount borrowed
questions.explanation: In the early years most of each repayment is interest, so the principal falls slowly at first and faster later. At the halfway point more than half of the principal is still owed.

questions.stem: A $300 000 loan at 6.6% p.a. compounded monthly runs for 10 years. How much more interest is paid to the lender if it is interest-only than if it is a reducing-balance loan?
questions.explanation: Interest-only costs 120 × $1650 = $198 000 in interest. The reducing-balance repayment is $3421.72, so its interest is $110 606.79. The difference is $87 393.21, the price of never reducing the principal.
